meta.audience: All the people of Zarahemla, assembled at the temple
meta.location: The temple in the land of Zarahemla

world_behind.title: The congregation answers, in unison
world_behind.text: Verse 2 has the whole multitude crying aloud with one voice, and the record gives their words. Assemblies in the Hebrew Bible answer their leaders, as at Sinai and under Ezra, and this is the record's fullest example. What they say is a request.

world_behind.title: A remission described as needing upkeep
world_behind.text: Verse 12 has them retaining a remission of sins; verse 26 makes the almsgiving a means of retaining it from day to day. The vocabulary treats forgiveness as a state that has to be held rather than an event that has happened, and nothing else in the record puts it quite this way.

world_behind.title: A poor law, argued from the giver's position
world_behind.text: Verses 16 through 25 work through the objection that the beggar deserves his condition, the answer that all are beggars, and then the case of a poor man who cannot give. Ancient legal codes legislate charity; this argues it, and it addresses the reluctant donor directly in the second person.

world_behind.title: The athletic figure
world_behind.text: Verse 27 puts running a race and winning a prize next to a warning against running faster than one has strength. Paul used the race for exertion; Benjamin uses it for pacing, and the sentence has become the record's standard caution against overreach.

world_behind.title: A borrowing rule, and a doubled sin
world_behind.text: Verse 28 says return what you borrowed as agreed, or you sin and may cause your neighbor to sin as well. It is the only piece of ordinary commercial ethics in the address, and the reason attached (the effect on the other man) is unusual for a debt provision.

words.text: Not abstinence from drink but seriousness: a steady, unexcited way of going about things. Benjamin tells parents to teach their children "to walk in the ways of truth and soberness" (v. 15). Paul reaches for the same pairing when he answers Festus with the words of truth and soberness. The King James Bible has the noun nowhere else. Set beside truth, it is about conduct rather than doctrine, and the same verse puts loving and serving one another next to it.

cites.quote: to walk in the ways of truth and soberness

spans.text: to walk in the ways of truth and soberness

words.text: To run to the aid of. The verb carries urgency in a way that "help" does not, and Alma will use it of Christ going to the aid of his people. Here it is what neighbors do for one another, described in the same breath as administering of one's substance.

The power to speak. In the New Testament it is what the Spirit hands out: tongues at Pentecost, boldness for Paul, a gift the Corinthians are told they are rich in. Benjamin reports the reverse. The Spirit was poured out, the people were filled with joy, and their "mouths should be stopped that ye could not find utterance" (v. 20). The gift arrives and what gets reported is the silence.

cites.quote: mouths should be stopped that ye could not find utterance

spans.text: mouths should be stopped that ye could not find utterance

words.text: Free of blame in a legal sense rather than innocent in a moral one. Benjamin applies it twice: to a poor man who gave nothing but meant to, and to anyone who imparts of his substance. What the word covers is standing, and a standing can be kept up from day to day.

A want is a lack. Benjamin says to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and visit the sick "according to their wants" (v. 26), meaning according to what those people are short of. Read with the modern sense the instruction turns into giving shaped by what the poor would like. That is not what it says. The King James Bible uses the plural twice, both times for what somebody does not have.

Various, several kinds. Benjamin says there are divers ways to sin, so many he cannot number them, and then stops trying. The admission closes the sermon's ethical section by conceding that no list would be complete.

phrases.term: They had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth
phrases.text: Benjamin had said in the previous chapter that they could not claim as much as the dust; the people go further and say less. The congregation's self-assessment outruns the king's, which is what makes the next clause a plea rather than a formality.

phrases.term: Apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness
phrases.text: A request phrased as an operation to be performed on them. The verb is transactional and the object is specific, and the whole sentence is spoken in one voice by a crowd that has just fallen to the ground. Nothing in it asks for a feeling.

phrases.term: Having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had
phrases.text: The result is named as conscience, and the cause is named as faith. The verse credits neither the falling nor the crying out. The phrase occurs once in scripture. What the people receive is the end of an accusation.

phrases.term: Awakened you to a sense of your nothingness, and your worthless and fallen state
phrases.text: The premise for everything that follows, and its trigger is knowledge of God's goodness. Benjamin makes the accurate self-view a consequence of seeing something good, which inverts the usual order.

phrases.term: The atonement which has been prepared from the foundation of the world
phrases.text: Prepared, and prepared before anything happened. Revelation calls the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world; Benjamin makes the same priority a matter of planning. The record uses the phrase eleven times and this is where it enters.

phrases.term: Believe in God; believe that he is
phrases.text: The list begins at the barest possible point and builds: that he is, that he created, that he has all wisdom and power, that we do not comprehend what he comprehends. Four propositions, the last of which is about the limits of the first three, and then verse 10 says do them.

phrases.term: Always retain in remembrance, the greatness of God, and your own nothingness
phrases.text: The noun occurs twice in this chapter and once in Helaman, and both times here Benjamin applies it to people who have just been forgiven. It is an accurate self-estimate that survives the good news instead of being removed by it. Two facts are held together, and the instruction is about retention. Benjamin is telling forgiven people to keep the estimate they had before they were forgiven, alongside the one they have now.

phrases.term: Ye will not suffer that the beggar putteth up his petition to you in vain
phrases.text: "Petition" is a legal word, a formal request made to authority, and it puts the beggar in the position of a claimant rather than a supplicant. Verse 22 will turn the same word around and ask what petition the withholder has put up.

phrases.term: The man has brought upon himself his misery; therefore I will stay my hand
phrases.text: The objection stated in full, in the objector's own voice, and it is the strongest version of it. Benjamin does not caricature the reluctant giver; he lets him finish the sentence, including the claim that the punishment is just. Then he answers.

Four words, and they dissolve the distinction the objection depends on. The argument is that the categories are wrong. Everyone lives on what was given, whether food, raiment, gold, or silver. It is the most quoted line Benjamin speaks.

phrases.term: Your substance, which doth not belong to you but to God
phrases.text: Ownership relocated in a subordinate clause. The withholder is not being asked to be generous with his own property; he is being told the property is not his, and the same sentence adds that his life is not either.

phrases.term: I give not because I have not, but if I had I would give
phrases.text: The poor man's script, supplied verbatim. Benjamin gives the words to say in the heart, and verse 25 says saying them keeps a person guiltless. It is the only place in the address where intention alone is made sufficient, and the reason is that nothing else is available.

phrases.term: It is not requisite that a man should run faster than he has strength
phrases.text: The negative construction carries it. Saying the running is not required makes the pacing a permission rather than an indulgence, and lifts a demand nobody had actually imposed. It is placed immediately after an instruction to feed, clothe, and visit according to their wants. The pacing clause is a limit on the preceding paragraph, and it arrives before anyone has had time to object. Diligence is required in the same verse; the two are held together by "order."

phrases.term: If ye do not watch yourselves, and your thoughts, and your words, and your deeds
phrases.text: Four objects of watching, moving from the person outward. The sermon's last instruction is surveillance of one's own interior, and the closing words, remember and perish not, are the shortest sentence Benjamin speaks.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The people answer
verses.text: The multitude has fallen to the earth; they see themselves as less than dust; they cry with one voice for the atoning blood to be applied; and the Spirit comes, joy follows, and they receive a remission with peace of conscience. Three verses, and they contain the only congregational speech in the address.

verses.label: v. 4–8
verses.title: The terms of salvation, restated
verses.text: Attention called again; if the goodness of God has awakened them to their nothingness; if they have come to know his goodness, power, wisdom, patience, and the atonement prepared before the world, then this is the man who is saved, and there are no other conditions. Benjamin closes the list explicitly.

verses.label: v. 9–12
verses.title: The list, and the instruction to act on it
verses.text: Four propositions about God, the last of which limits the first three; then repent, forsake, humble yourself, ask sincerely; and if you believe all this, do it. The reward named is retention. Always rejoice, always retain, and grow.

verses.label: v. 13–16
verses.title: What retention looks like
verses.text: No mind to injure, peaceable living, rendering each his due; children not hungry or naked and not left to quarrel or serve the devil; children taught truth, soberness, love, and service; and neighbors succored, substance administered, the beggar not turned away. The doctrine becomes a household code.

verses.label: v. 17–19
verses.title: The objection, and the answer
verses.text: He brought it on himself, so I will stay my hand. The reply is that whoever says this has great cause to repent, and then comes the question that removes the ground: are we not all beggars? Three verses, and the middle one is the harshest sentence in the chapter.

verses.label: v. 20–26
verses.title: Begging, both directions
verses.text: They have just been begging for a remission and were not refused; God grants what is rightly asked; therefore impart. If you judge the petitioner, your own condemnation is greater, and the substance was never yours. Woe to the rich who withhold; and to the poor who cannot give, a sentence to say in the heart. Then the summary: feed, clothe, visit, relieve, both spiritually and temporally.

verses.label: v. 27–30
verses.title: Order, and the last word
verses.text: Wisdom and order, no running faster than strength, diligence to win the prize; return what you borrow or you sin and may cause another to; the ways to sin are past numbering; and finally, watch yourself and continue to the end. "Remember, and perish not."

chapter.title: The people speak, and what they say is a request
chapter.text: The only congregational line in the whole address asks for the atoning blood to be applied. They do not promise, agree, or thank. The covenant comes in Mosiah 5; here the crowd asks for something and receives it in the next verse.

chapter.title: Nothingness survives the forgiveness
chapter.text: Benjamin tells people who have just been filled with joy to retain in remembrance their own nothingness alongside God's greatness. The chapter's account of a healthy inner life keeps both estimates running at once, and it makes the second the condition of keeping the first.

chapter.title: Remission is treated as something maintained
chapter.text: Retain a remission, retain it from day to day, walk guiltless. The grammar throughout is continuous. Almsgiving is offered as the means, which ties the interior state to a repeated external act.

chapter.title: The objection to charity is given its strongest form
chapter.text: Verse 17 lets the reluctant giver make his case completely, including the claim that the suffering is deserved. Benjamin's answer does not dispute the facts of the case; it disputes the standing of the person making it.

chapter.title: Ownership is the hinge of the argument
chapter.text: The substance does not belong to the giver, and neither does his life. Once that is granted, withholding becomes misappropriation, which is why the language turns to condemnation and petitions and woe.

chapter.title: The poor are addressed too, and given words
chapter.text: Verse 24 supplies a sentence for those who have nothing to give, and verse 25 makes saying it enough. The chapter is careful to require that the intention be real (covet instead and you are condemned), but it asks for nothing a person without means cannot produce.

chapter.title: The sermon ends by lifting a burden it just imposed
chapter.text: Feed, clothe, visit, relieve. Then, in the next verse, do not run faster than you have strength. Benjamin puts the limit inside the command, and pairs it with diligence so that neither swallows the other.

applications.title: Make it a request
applications.text: The crowd asked for something to be applied to them. When you next want to change, start by asking for what you cannot do yourself.

applications.title: Hold both estimates
applications.text: Write down, on one page, something true about God's greatness and something true about your own smallness. Benjamin's instruction is to keep both in view at once, permanently.

applications.title: Retain the remission
applications.text: Treat forgiveness as something to be kept up. Identify the daily practice that does the keeping for you, and notice that Benjamin's answer was giving to someone poorer.

applications.title: Let the objection finish
applications.text: Before answering an argument you disagree with, state it as strongly as its holder would. Benjamin does this and then answers the person who holds it.

applications.title: Say the sentence if you cannot give
applications.text: If you genuinely have nothing, the chapter supplies the words. Say them honestly, and check whether what follows in you is peace or envy.

applications.title: Set your own pace, and keep it
applications.text: Find the thing you have been doing at an unsustainable rate in the name of duty, and slow it to a rate you can hold. The verse requires diligence in the same breath, so slowing is not stopping.

applications.title: Return what you borrowed
applications.text: Literally. Make the list, and return the things, this week.

questions.text: When did I last ask for something spiritual instead of resolving to do better?
Does knowing God is good make me more honest about myself, or more defensive?
Am I trying to get forgiven again, or to keep what I was given?
Whose misery have I decided is deserved, and what does that decision do for me?
If everything I have was given, what exactly am I protecting?
If I have little to give, is what is in my heart generosity or envy?
What am I doing faster than I have strength for, and who told me to?
